rows.title: Speed
rows.text: If you are a cane toad, a light that flashes faster than about 7 times a second looks steady to you, where a human needs about 60 flashes a second before it looks steady. Other Rhinella toads, the cane toad's relatives in the same genus, very likely have a similarly low limit. Nobody has measured it in most other frogs and toads.
rows.note: Only R1 (cane toad, 6.7 Hz) exists; the number is kept to the cane toad and the Rhinella sentence carries only the general ability.

rows.title: Field of view, sharpness and pupil
rows.text: If you are a bullfrog, green frog, northern leopard frog, European common frog or European toad, your pupil is a horizontal almond-shaped slit, though a red-eyed treefrog has an upright one. If you are a northern leopard frog, you see about 3 cycles a degree, about a tenth of the 30 a human reads on an eye chart, and nobody has measured this in most other frogs and toads. Nobody has measured how wide your field of view is.
rows.note: No record gives a field of view for any frog or toad, so the row says so.

failed.title: Movement
failed.last: If you are a cane toad, you strike at a moving model of an insect. If you are a bullfrog, you start to avoid an object coming straight at you when it looks about 20 degrees wide to you. If you are a European toad, the nerve cells that pick out moving prey respond less when a black and white textured background moves along with the prey at the same speed. Nobody has measured how most other frogs and toads detect movement.
